title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (3 of 7)
hook: a text about letting go that tells you to live a hundred years, working
tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (4 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second half of the first verse: tyaktena; let them go when they go. By that renounced, enjoy; do not covet; whose is wealth? Did you use one thing like a guest? Day two hundred thirty-four.

Here's the obvious objection to yesterday. If everything belongs to the Lord, and the wise thing is to let go, why not just quit? Leave the job, leave the inbox, go sit under a tree. Some people in the tradition have done exactly that, and they're honored for it. But the very next verse of the Isha doesn't say quit. It says something closer to the opposite. And it's the verse that makes this tiny Upanishad a favorite of people with rent to pay.
screen: `WHY NOT JUST QUIT?` → `THE NEXT VERSE.` → `NOT THE ANSWER YOU EXPECT.`

segments.voice: Verse two: kurvann eveha karmani jijivishet shatam samah. Doing works here, one may wish to live a hundred years. Karmani is actions, works, the same karma you learned on day nine: action, and what it grows. Shatam samah is a hundred years, the full human life in the old Vedic hope. So the text that just said let go now says: live long, and keep working. Then it gives the reason. For you, living this way, there is no other way; action does not cling to a person. The word for cling pictures something smeared on, like oil or mud. Actions done in the spirit of verse one, knowing all this belongs to the Lord, don't stick. You do them, and they don't glue themselves to you. That's the seed of the Gita's whole idea of karma yoga, which you spent weeks with: act fully, and don't cling to the fruit. Here it is centuries earlier, in two lines. Verse three is darker. It speaks of worlds called asurya, covered in blind darkness, and says those who are killers of the self go there. Some translators hear asurya as sunless; others, Shankara among them, as the worlds of the asuras. Either way, it's dark. Most commentators don't read that as literal suicide. They read it as people who live as if the self weren't there at all, who bury the light under grabbing. So the three verses stack up. All this is the Lord's. Enjoy it by letting go. And keep working, a hundred years if you get them, without letting the work stick to you. Renounce, and enjoy, and get up tomorrow.
screen: `DOING WORKS HERE.` · `LIVE A HUNDRED YEARS.` · `ACTION DOES NOT CLING.` · `THE WORLDS OF BLIND DARKNESS.` · then, large: `RENOUNCE, AND KEEP WORKING.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Bring to mind one task waiting for you today. Something ordinary: a report, the dishes, a phone call. See yourself doing it well. Now see yourself finishing it, and letting it go, the way you'd wash oil off your hands. Not carrying it into the next hour. Breathe in as you picture the work. Breathe out as you picture it done and released. If your mind runs to the result, how it'll be judged, notice that, and come back to the doing. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, works. Verse two adds: and keep working. Doing works here, wish to live a hundred years; action done this way doesn't cling.
Your line: don't let the work stick. Today, do one job fully, then wash your hands of it. Don't take it to dinner. Day two hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often cite Isha verse 2 to show that the Upanishads do not require leaving the world: a householder can work a full life without being bound by the work.

match.prompt: verses two and three — tap the pairs.

myth: the Isha tells everyone to quit their work and withdraw
verse two says doing works here, one may wish to live a hundred years.
the Isha's idea of action that doesn't cling comes centuries before the Gita
verse two plants the seed the Gita grows into karma yoga.
most commentators read 'killers of the self' in verse three as literal suicide
most read it as living as if the self weren't there, hiding the light.

fork.setup: you've understood that all this belongs to the Lord. what does verse two tell you to do next?
options: stop acting, since nothing is yours.
keep doing your work, a hundred years if you get them.
act only for what you'll gain.
fork.reveal: keep working. done this way, the text says, action does not cling to you.

original.note: Sanskrit: karma, action; verse two uses karmani, works, from the root kri, to do.

trapdoor: what you thought: letting go means dropping out.
what it means: the Isha says keep working, and let the work not stick to you.
what a scholar hears: kurvann eveha karmani jijivishet shatam samah; the verb for cling (lip) means to smear, as with oil.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 2 (doing works, live a hundred years; action does not cling)
Isha Upanishad 3 (the sunless worlds; killers of the self)

notes: Verse 2's 'na karma lipyate nare': the cling verb as 'smear' (lip) — check.
Verse 3 'atmahano': reading as those who ignore the self, not literal suicide — check commentators (Shankara reads it as those ignorant of the self).
Claim that the Isha predates the Gita: consensus dating, but phrase 'centuries earlier' should be checked.

Audit (second sample): the teach glossed asurya flatly as 'sunless'. The word as usually printed (asuryā) is read by Shankara and many translators as 'of the asuras', and 'sunless' (a-sūrya) is a second, popular reading; the teach now gives both, and the match pair no longer asserts 'sunless'. The teach screen head now reads THE WORLDS OF BLIND DARKNESS.
